article_sentences: Cyclone Akvan is expected to bring heavy to extremely heavy rainfall across seven states, with Tamil Nadu, Odisha, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh among the regions facing weather warnings.

The storm is expected to cross the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts around noon on November 20, with wind speeds reaching 130 kmph and gusts of up to 145 kmph.

The system was centred near latitude 12.2°N and longitude 85.7°E.
It was located approximately 610 km east of Chennai, 660 km southeast of Machilipatnam, 670 km south-southeast of Visakhapatnam and 790 km south of Gopalpur in Odisha.
The IMD expects the cyclone to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm by Tuesday evening and further strengthen into a very severe cyclonic storm around the morning of November 19.
Continuing its northwestward movement, the storm is likely to cross the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Nellore and Tuni around noon on November 20.
The maximum sustained wind speed is expected to reach 120-130 kmph, with gusts touching 145 kmph.

stories.headline: Cyclone Akvan Alert: Atchanna orders steps for safety of farmers and fishermen
stories.title: Cyclone Akvan Alert: Atchanna orders steps for safety of farmers and fishermen
stories.summary: Puts officials on high alert to shield crops and fishermen from heavy rains and strong winds Nearly all fishing boats safely ashore; coastal paddy and horticulture under special focus
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Amaravati: Agriculture and fisheries minister K Atchannaidu directed officials to remain on high alert and take precautionary measures to protect farmers, crops and fishermen in view of the heavy rains and strong winds forecast under Cyclone Akwan.
He stressed that the coalition government would stand by farmers and fishermen during the crisis.
As of November 14, kharif crops were standing on 21.32 lakh hectares and rabi crops covered 2.55 lakh hectares, taking the total cropped area to 23.87 lakh hectares.
Paddy accounted for 13.60 lakh hectares, red gram 4.42 lakh hectares and cotton 1.92 lakh hectares.
Special attention was directed towards 9.51 lakh hectares of crops in 10 coastal districts, including 9.16 lakh hectares of paddy.
Farmers were advised to harvest ready crops, clear field drains and avoid spraying fertilisers and pesticides during heavy rainfall.
Officials were also asked to protect 2,69,831 hectares of horticultural crops across 16 districts, including 1,08,615 hectares of chilli, 98,526 hectares of coconut and 24,469 hectares of turmeric.
Protective support should be provided to banana and papaya plants, while ready produce should be moved to markets.
The Minister said 30,635 of the 30,808 fishing boats had safely returned to shore by 10 am on November 16, while the remaining 173 boats were being monitored.
Around 1,08,250 voice alerts had been sent to fishermen, and 8,217 boats were being tracked through the Nabhimitra system.
Surveillance was intensified across 555 fishing villages and 350 landing centres.
Aquaculture farmers were advised to strengthen pond bunds and monitor water quality.

stories.headline: Suspicious movement near LoC in Poonch’s Saujiyan
stories.title: Suspicious movement near LoC in Poonch’s Saujiyan
stories.summary: Poonch Mandi, Nov 16: Army troops opened fire after noticing suspicious movement near the Line of Control (LoC) in the Saujiyan area of Poonch district during the intervening night of Sunday and Monday, triggering a search operation in the area. A senior police officer said suspicious movement was noticed near the LoC in the Kanari area of Sujiyan, following which Army personnel fired to neutralise any potential threat. Following the incident, Army and other security agencies were put on high alert, with surveillance intensified along sensitive locations in the area. Security forces have launched a search operation to ascertain the nature of the suspicious movement and establish whether it was linked to a possible infiltration attempt. The search operation was underway in the Sawjian sector till the filing of this report.

stories.headline: CS Ladakh reviews upcoming election preparedness
stories.title: CS Ladakh reviews upcoming election preparedness
stories.summary: Leh, Nov 16: Chief Secretary, Ladakh Union Territory Ashish Kundra Monday chaired a meeting to review the arrangements and preparedness for the upcoming elections of Panchayat, Municipal and LAHDCs. During the meeting, various election-related arrangements were also discussed which included availability and management of ballot boxes, printing of ballot papers, arrangements concerning EVMs, installation of CCTV cameras at designated locations, heating facilities, transportation and other logistical requirements to ensure the smooth conduct of elections. The Chief Secretary emphasised the importance of timely completion of both physical and digital arrangements and directed the concerned departments and district administrations to ensure that all necessary facilities are put in place well in advance. He also reviewed preparations concerning service voters, SVEEP (Systematic Voters’ Education and Electoral Participation) activities, and arrangements for the counting of votes, including coordination regarding the counting date. The Chief Secretary directed all concerned officers to maintain close coordination with the State Election Commission, strengthen district-level monitoring and ensure that all election-related arrangements are completed within the stipulated timelines for the smooth, free and fair conduct of the upcoming LAHDC elections in Ladakh. During the meeting, the Chief Secretary took a detailed review of the constituency-wise and district-wise status of nomination filing and enquired about the number of nominations received so far, the candidates who had collected nomination papers and the expected nominations in the coming days. He directed the concerned Deputy Commissioners to provide regular updates on nominations received in their respective districts and ensure close coordination with all stakeholders to facilitate the smooth completion of the nomination process. The meeting was attended by the Director General of Police Ladakh UT, Divisional Commissioner Ladakh UT, Secretary Rural Development Department, Chief Electoral Officer Ladakh UT, all Deputy Commissioners, all District SSPs/SPs, State Informatics Officer and Additional State Informatics Officers, NIC, UT Ladakh, and Rigzin Spalgon who is the nodal officer for coordination with the State Election Commission. Officers stationed outside Leh participated in the meeting through Video Conference.

stories.headline: Security forces must not be dragged into political narratives: Adv Purnima Sharma
stories.title: Security forces must not be dragged into political narratives: Adv Purnima Sharma
stories.summary: Jammu, Nov 16: BJP spokespersons Advocate Purnima Sharma and Rajni Sethi Monday criticised Jammu and Kashmir Pradesh Congress Committee (JKPCC) President Tariq Hameed Karra over his controversial remarks concerning the martyrdom of two Special Police Officers (SPOs) in Kishtwar. They said such statements expose Congress's irresponsible approach towards national security. Addressing a press conference at the BJP headquarters Trikuta Nagar, Jammu, BJP demanded a fair, transparent and impartial investigation into the incident. They said Karra's attempt to suggest that Army personnel mistook the SPOs for militants and shot them, even before the investigation has reached a conclusion was "highly objectionable." J&K BJP Media Incharge Dr. Pardeep Mahotra, Advocate Purnima Sharma were also present at the media briefing. Sharma questioned how a senior political leader could publicly suggest that the SPOs were mistaken for militants and shot by Army personnel, reportedly relying on an account attributed to a Congress district president. “Has Congress established its own parallel investigation agency? Who has authorised Tariq Hameed Karra to pronounce conclusions before the official investigation is complete? If Congress possesses credible evidence, it should submit it to the appropriate authorities instead of conducting a political trial through press statements,” Sharma said. She said that making unverified allegations against the Army not only undermines public confidence in security institutions but also demoralizes personnel serving under extremely challenging circumstances. She said that the security forces deserve respect and support, not politically motivated insinuations. Taking aim at Congress's political legacy, Sharma recalled the Emergency imposed in 1975, the 1984 anti-Sikh riots and former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi's controversial remark, “When a big tree falls, the earth shakes.” She said Congress must answer for its own record on democracy and national security before lecturing others on constitutional values. She also questioned the party's approach during decades of terrorism and separatist violence in Jammu and Kashmir. Rajni Sethi also condemned the Congress leaders' remarks questioning the Army's role in the Kishtwar incident. She said whether Congress was deliberately attempting to create communal tensions and weaken the country's internal security for narrow political gains. Recalling Congress's repeated questioning of the armed forces after the Uri surgical strikes and Balakot airstrike, Sethi said the party had repeatedly displayed a tendency to politicize matters concerning national security. Referring to Sonia Gandhi's memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, she said its references to the Emergency imposed by Indira Gandhi and the Babri Masjid demolition, along with the acknowledgement that the Emergency was a mistake, raise questions about Congress's democratic legacy and its tendency to place family and political interests above democratic values. She also criticised Congress for repeatedly questioning institutions like the CBI, Election Commission and ED whenever their functioning does not suit its political interests. Commenting on the Bharat Summit in Telangana, attended by nearly 1000 delegates from around 70 countries, Sethi said that domestic political differences should never be allowed to damage India's international image. Both leaders demanded that Karra must produce credible evidence to substantiate his allegations or tender an unconditional apology to the nation, particularly the people of J&K. They asked the Congress high command to clarify whether Karra's remarks represent the party's official position. They said the martyrdom of the two SPOs must unite every responsible political voice against terrorism rather than become an opportunity for political point-scoring. "The bereaved families deserve justice through an impartial investigation, while the dignity of the Army and national security must remain above party politics," they said.

stories.title: No proof from ECI to show SIR was a ‘unanimous’ decision, Rahul Gandhi to Supreme Court
stories.summary: The ECI’s October 26 affidavit, in response to a petition filed by INDIA bloc leaders led by Mr. Gandhi, denied any differences of opinion between the CEC and the Election Commissioners over the SIR process
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi told the Supreme Court on Monday (November 16, 2026) that the Election Commission of India (ECI) failed to produce any proof to establish its claim that the special intensive revision (SIR) was a “unanimous” decision made by Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.

“No minutes of the meeting, file notings, recorded approvals, agenda, deliberations or other primary material evidencing the participation and approval of all three members have been produced with the ECI counter-affidavit of October 26,” Mr. Gandhi submitted in his rejoinder.

Mr. Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders have also separately filed an application containing a set of “interrogatories” directed at the CEC, the two Election Commissioners, and other senior ECI officials involved in the SIR.

The pointed questions inquire about the number and details of each SIR file, as well as the specific occasions between February 19, 2025, and October 26, 2026, on which the two Election Commissioners objected in writing or expressed dissent or reservation regarding any matter related to the SIR, ECINET, Form 6, or the filing of appeals.
The case is scheduled for hearing on November 17 before a Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant.

The reported friction between Mr. Kumar and the two Election Commissioners over the SIR and the CEC’s allegedly unilateral and authoritarian conduct, had triggered widespread protests across India demanding his removal from office.

The ECI’s October 26 affidavit, in response to a petition filed by INDIA bloc leaders led by Mr. Gandhi, denied any differences of opinion between the CEC and the Election Commissioners over the SIR process.
Mr. Gandhi said the court must not accept such “bare assertions” from the ECI.
He questioned why the affidavit was filed by the ECI when Mr. Kumar, Mr. Sandhu and Mr. Joshi were separately made respondents.
The Opposition leader, represented by senior advocate.
A.M. Singhvi and advocate Prasanna S., said the EC chose not to explain when and where exactly the decision to conduct a nationwide SIR was made.

The ECI affidavit’s blank assertions contradict its own Right to Information (RTI) response that “the Commission has so far not taken any decision on initiating a special intensive revision (SIR) across the country in 2025”.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court has suspended the life sentences and granted bail to two convicts in the Bilkis Bano gangrape and murder case, noting that they have spent more than 17 years in prison and that one of them suffers from a severe handicap.

A Bench of Justices MM Sundresh and Prasanna B Varale passed the order on October 28, granting relief to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya, who had challenged the Bombay High Court's May 2017 judgment upholding their conviction and life sentences.
The order was uploaded to the Supreme Court's website recently.
The Bench, while granting bail, observed that the two appellants had been incarcerated for more than 17 years and that one of them suffered from a severe handicap.
The court also noted that their appeal involved questions of fact and law that required consideration.

“Having heard the parties, it suffices to state that the appellants have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years, and also the fact remains that one of the appellants has a severe handicap.
Certainly, there are issues to be decided in the appeal, both on fact and law.

In view of the above and considering the issues involved in this appeal, we suspend the sentence and grant bail to the appellants on such terms and conditions as may be imposed by the trial court,” the Bench said.

He also submitted that Joshi, who had undergone leg surgery, was severely handicapped.

It was also submitted that no specific overt act had been attributed to them and that the evidence against them primarily concerned their alleged presence in the mob at the time of the incident.

stories.headline: J&K’s mountains need governance that works, not just another policy
stories.title: J&K’s mountains need governance that works, not just another policy
stories.summary: Jammu and Kashmir’s mountains are not simply scenic backdrops for tourism. They are living ecological systems that sustain our rivers, springs, forests, agriculture, horticulture, biodiversity and communities. Their health is inseparable from our economic security. But the very landscapes on which our prosperity depends are facing mounting pressure from unplanned construction, poorly designed roads, unmanaged waste, water stress, growing visitor numbers and increasing climate-related risks. The proposed Jammu and Kashmir Sustainable Mountain Development Policy (SMDP) 2026 offers an opportunity to address these challenges. Its ambition to connect ecological protection, tourism, infrastructure, disaster risk and livelihoods is timely. But one question must be asked before another policy framework is added to an already crowded institutional landscape. Is the principal problem the absence of policy, or the failure to integrate and implement what we already have? My review of the existing policy and legal architecture suggests that Jammu and Kashmir is not starting from zero. The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Water Act, 1974, the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, forest and wildlife safeguards, the J&K State Disaster Management Policy, 2018, and the Tourism Policy, 2020 already provide important foundations. The challenge is that these instruments often operate through separate departments, plans and approval processes, while mountain ecosystems function as connected landscapes. The SMDP should therefore become an instrument of governance integration and not another parallel regulatory structure. The world’s mountains offer practical lessons International experience provides useful guidance, although no model can simply be copied into Jammu and Kashmir. The Alpine Convention is perhaps the strongest example of a coordinated mountain-governance framework. It brings together eight Alpine countries and the European Union through a framework convention supported by protocols covering spatial planning, nature conservation, mountain forests, tourism, transport, energy and soil protection. Its significance lies not in creating one institution to control every activity, but in establishing shared principles and mechanisms for cooperation across sectors and borders. Its periodic Reports on the State of the Alps also provide a basis for monitoring ecological, economic and social change. The Alpine Convention and its spatiall planning framework offer lessons for J&K. The practical message is clear. A road, hotel, tourism facility or hydropower project cannot be assessed only within the boundaries of the department approving it. Its cumulative impact on slopes, forests, drainage, water availability and settlements must be considered at landscape level. For J&K, this means connecting district plans, protected-area management, tourism planning, road development and watershed management through a common mountain framework. Bhutan offers a different lesson. Its tourism model has used a Sustainable Development Fee to support national development and environmental priorities. The fee is linked to a broader tourism philosophy, while Bhutan’s own tourism authorities have also undertaken work on tourism carrying capacity. The important lesson is not that J&K should copy Bhutan’s charges or its high-value, low-volume model. Bhutan has a different geography, economy, institutional structure and tourism profile. Rather, J&K should learn that tourism revenue must be connected to a transparent public purpose, and that visitor management must consider environmental, cultural, social and economic conditions together. Bhutan’s tourism rules and its official sustainable Development fee provide useful reference points. Nepal’s community forestry experience offers another important lesson: conservation is more durable when local people have a meaningful role in managing natural resources and sharing benefits. A 2025 World Bank report records a rise in Nepal’s forest cover from 29 per cent in 1994 to more than 46 per cent in 2022, attributing much of the progress to community-based forest management. It also cautions that forest degradation, unequal access and data gaps remain,which precipitated in the shape of recent Nepal floods.The lesson for J&K is that local participation cannot be reduced to consultation after decisions have been made. Mountain communities must be partners in planning, monitoring, restoration and livelihood development.. These experiences point towards a common principle. Mountain governance succeeds when ecological limits, spatial planning, local institutions, finance and accountability reinforce one another. Carrying capacity must be scientific, not arbitrary The discussion around visitor limits at Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Sonamarg and other destinations has rightly drawn attention to tourism pressure. However, carrying capacity cannot be reduced to the number of vehicles a road or parking area can accommodate. A destination’s real capacity depends on several interdependent factors. These include reliable drinking water, wastewater treatment, solid-waste collection and processing, road congestion, parking, biodiversity sensitivity, seasonal variation, emergency response and evacuation capacity. A place may accommodate a large number of visitors on a particular day but still be unable to manage the resulting sewage, water demand or ecological disturbance. The United Nations Environment Programme and IUCN guidance on sustainable tourism in protected areas emphasises visitor management within the limits set by environmental and social conditions. Jammu and Kashmir should adopt destination-specific carrying-capacity assessments, beginning with the most pressured and ecologically sensitive locations. These should establish measurable thresholds for water consumption, sewage generation, waste handling, traffic, ecological disturbance and emergency services. Visitor registration, time-slot bookings, shuttle systems or temporary restrictions may be appropriate where the evidence supports them. Thresholds should be reviewed as conditions change, with transparent triggers for reducing access or temporarily closing a site. Blanket caps without credible baseline studies risk becoming arbitrary restrictions. They may also affect the livelihoods of local transport operators, guides, pony handlers, homestay owners and small businesses. Visitor management must therefore be accompanied by a fair transition plan and viable local alternatives. There is already a useful legal starting point. The Eco-Sensitive Zone notification of 16 May 2024 for the Dachigam–Overa-Aru–Thajwas landscape provides for a Zonal Master Plan and a Tourism Master Plan based on carrying-capacity assessment, alongside ecological safeguards and risk assessment. The immediate task should be to verify the status and implementation of these requirements and use the experience to inform planning elsewhere. Infrastructure must respect the mountain One of the most visible failures of mountain development is the assumption that engineering practices suited to plains can be transferred to steep and fragile terrain. Unscientific hill cutting, inadequate drainage, indiscriminate muck disposal and poorly planned road widening can destabilise slopes and increase exposure to landslides. A road that is cheaper to construct but repeatedly damaged by rainfall is not economical. It merely transfers the cost to public budgets and communities. Mountain infrastructure needs a different set of standards. Before approval, projects should undergo geotechnical, hydrological, seismic and climate-risk screening. Road designs must account for slope stability, drainage, cut-and-fill limits, safe muck disposal and slope restoration. Stream corridors, unstable slopes, glacier forelands and other high-risk areas should be subject to no-build or restricted-development provisions based on scientific mapping. Tourism infrastructure must also follow a basic rule. Accommodation should not expand beyond the destination’s capacity to provide safe water, treat sewage and manage waste. Sewage-treatment and waste-processing arrangements must precede additional accommodation, not follow it. Cumulative-impact assessment is equally important. A series of individually approved projects can collectively damage a watershed or destabilise a landscape. The SMDP should require development decisions to consider the combined pressure of roads, hotels, commercial establishments, utilities and visitor activity. Finance, institutions and local accountability The reported proposals associated with the draft SMDP including visitor limits, green gateways, a Mountain Green Cess, a dedicated fund and a proposed Mountain Development Authority deserve careful examination. Newspaper reports have described these measures A green cess could help finance ecological restoration, sanitation, waste management and visitor safety. But it must have a clear legal basis, transparent rates, defined exemptions and destination-wise accounting. Revenue collected in the name of environmental protection should produce visible environmental outcomes. Annual public accounts and independent audits should show what was collected, where it was spent and what improved. Similarly, a new authority should not duplicate the powers of existing statutory regulators or create another layer of permissions. Before establishing one, the government should map existing mandates and identify the precise coordination failures that cannot be resolved through strengthened departmental mechanisms. If a new institution is justified, its powers, accountability, relationship with existing agencies and reporting obligations must be explicit. Local communities should have formal representation in destination-level planning and monitoring. A proportion of tourism-related revenue should support local employment, waste services, ecological restoration, community infrastructure and disaster preparedness. Cooperatives and local enterprises can operate transport, guiding, waste-management and visitor services, provided procurement and licensing remain transparent. From policy promises to measurable outcomes My perspective on this issue is shaped by several decades of work in environmental science and public institutions in Jammu and Kashmir. I began with field research on land-use patterns in the Karewa belt, soil erosion and the condition of waters around Nilnag and Yusmarg. Later, as the first Board Analyst of the J&K State Pollution Control Board, I worked on air and water monitoring, laboratories and consent-management systems. I was involved in Wular Lake conservation and management, preparation of the State’s first State of Environment Report and the J&K State Action Plan on Climate Change. I also served as an environmental expert on the World Bank-assisted Jhelum and Tawi Flood Recovery Project. These experiences have taught me that scientific knowledge is valuable only when it informs decisions, institutions have the capacity to act, and implementation can be monitored. A report cannot protect a lake if its catchment continues to be degraded. A climate plan cannot reduce vulnerability if infrastructure approvals ignore risk. And a mountain policy cannot succeed if departments continue to work in isolation. The SMDP should begin with a public legal and institutional audit. It should then establish ecological, hydrological, land-use and hazard baselines for priority landscapes. A small number of diverse destinations could be selected for demonstration projects, with measurable standards for water, waste, transport, construction, visitor management and community benefits. Successful models should be independently evaluated before wider expansion. An annual Mountain Sustainability Scorecard should report nine core indicators. These are ecological and habitat condition; forest, watershed and spring health; water availability and wastewater treatment; waste generation and processing; visitor pressure against assessed capacity; infrastructure and slope-risk compliance; warning and evacuation readiness; local employment and benefit-sharing; and destination-wise budgets and verified outcomes. Where data are missing, the scorecard should say so. Transparent gaps are more useful than misleading claims of progress. Jammu and Kashmir has an opportunity to demonstrate that mountain development can be both economically productive and ecologically responsible. The objective should not be to stop tourism or development, but to ensure that neither destroys the natural systems on which they depend. Our mountains do not need another document that repeats familiar commitments. They need decisions guided by science, institutions that coordinate, infrastructure designed for the terrain, communities that share in the benefits and public systems that can be held accountable. The real measure of the Sustainable Mountain Development Policy will not be how many new provisions or authorities it creates. It will be whether our springs remain alive, our slopes remain stable, our rivers remain cleaner, our destinations remain habitable and mountain communities enjoy secure livelihoods. Strengthen existing institutions, implement existing obligations and create new powers only where a demonstrable gap remains. That is how Jammu and Kashmir can move from policy proliferation to integrated mountain and climate governance. Mutaharra A W Deva, Certified Independent Director from Indian institute of Corporate Affairs, Ministry of Corporate affairs Government of India.

stories.title: The Home-Grown Paradox
stories.summary: TECHNOLOGY & NATIONAL SECURITY Imagine a defence office being told it can no longer use ChatGPT, Gemini or any other foreign AI tool. Only Indian-made AI is allowed. That may soon be real. On 9 November, Business Standard reported that the Centre is likely to push government-run critical sectors, especially defence and aerospace, towards home-grown AI models. One official told the paper that departments could be asked to avoid foreign frontier AI altogether. No ministry has confirmed this on record, and no order has been issued. The idea is easy to like. Why should India’s secrets pass through tools owned by American or Chinese companies? But there is a catch. A rule meant to make us safer could leave our most important offices with weaker tools, while the real weak point stays exactly where it was. What India has built so far The government’s IndiaAI Mission has a budget of about ₹10,372 crore. Under it, 20 AI models from 12 Indian startups have been approved, according to the same report. Some are already out: models from Sarvam and BharatGen, Soket’s EKA-1, and ZenteiQ’s Dhir models. This is real progress. The armed forces are also building their own AI systems that run without the internet, Business Standard noted. The 80 per cent problem Here is the uncomfortable part. An unnamed official claimed some Indian models now reach up to 80 per cent of what the world’s best models can do. No test or benchmark was named, so we cannot check that number. Even if it is true, think about what 80 per cent means. For writing a school essay, it is fine. For a defence analyst summarising intelligence reports, the missing 20 per cent is where mistakes hide. A wrong summary in a military office is far more dangerous than a data leak that never happens. So the risk does not disappear. It changes shape. We stop worrying about who can see our data and start worrying about whether the answer is right. “An Indian brain running on American chips is still a borrowed body.” The chips are still foreign An AI model is software. It needs powerful computer chips to run. In March, Minister of State Jitin Prasada told the Lok Sabha that more than 38,000 of these chips, called GPUs, had been added to the mission’s shared computing pool. A July report in Communications Today said most of them are Nvidia H100 and H200 units. Nvidia is an American company. This matters because chip sales are political. On 13 November, Reuters reported that US lawmakers are pushing for tougher controls on selling advanced AI chips abroad. The target is China, not India. Still, it is a reminder that the tap for these chips sits in Washington. A made-in-India model does not change that. Money is also moving slowly. Government figures given in the Rajya Sabha, as reported by MediaNama, showed ₹379 crore released in 2025-26 against a revised estimate of ₹800 crore. As of April, nothing had been released from this year’s ₹1,000 crore budget. Will it understand Kashmiri? For readers here, there is a more local question. Indian AI is sold as AI that understands Indian languages. But most of the attention goes to Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and Marathi. Kashmiri work has mostly come from small efforts. NIT Srinagar’s Gaash Lab ran a national challenge in August to build English-to-Kashmiri translation tools, Kashmir Life reported. AI4Bharat has put a Kashmiri speech-recognition model on the government’s AIKosh platform. And a young developer from Pulwama, Saqlain Yousuf, built a Kashmiri chatbot on his own, without funding, as this newspaper reported in February 2025. If government offices are later told to use only Indian models, people in Kashmir will deal with those systems for forms, complaints and services. A model that handles Hindi well but stumbles on Kashmiri is not much help in Pulwama or Baramulla. Bottom Line Wanting our own AI is sensible. But a rule that forces critical offices to switch before the tools are proven could swap one risk for another. Before any such order, the government should publish how these models perform on real tests, name which languages they truly support, and admit openly that the chips underneath still come from abroad. Sovereignty that only covers the software is half a job. The other half is the hardware underneath, and the languages people here actually speak. ( The author is studying Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence at Rutgers University, New Jersey, USA. He is interested in emerging technologies and innovation, and can be reached on LinkedIn at @arssh-kumar14)

A rule meant to make us safer could leave our most important offices with weaker tools, while the real weak point stays exactly where it was.
What India has built so far.
The government’s IndiaAI Mission has a budget of about ₹10,372 crore.
Under it, 20 AI models from 12 Indian startups have been approved, according to the same report.
Some are already out: models from Sarvam and BharatGen, Soket’s EKA-1, and ZenteiQ’s Dhir models.
This is real progress.
The armed forces are also building their own AI systems that run without the internet, Business Standard noted.
The 80 per cent problem Here is the uncomfortable part.
An unnamed official claimed some Indian models now reach up to 80 per cent of what the world’s best models can do.
No test or benchmark was named, so we cannot check that number.
Even if it is true, think about what 80 per cent means.
For writing a school essay, it is fine.
For a defence analyst summarising intelligence reports, the missing 20 per cent is where mistakes hide.
A wrong summary in a military office is far more dangerous than a data leak that never happens.
So the risk does not disappear.
It changes shape.
We stop worrying about who can see our data and start worrying about whether the answer is right.
“An Indian brain running on American chips is still a borrowed body.” The chips are still foreign.
An AI model is software.
It needs powerful computer chips to run.
In March, Minister of State Jitin Prasada told the Lok Sabha that more than 38,000 of these chips, called GPUs, had been added to the mission’s shared computing pool.
A July report in Communications Today said most of them are Nvidia H100 and H200 units.
Nvidia is an American company.
This matters because chip sales are political.
On 13 November, Reuters reported that US lawmakers are pushing for tougher controls on selling advanced AI chips abroad.
The target is China, not India.
Still, it is a reminder that the tap for these chips sits in Washington.
A made-in-India model does not change that.
Money is also moving slowly.
Government figures given in the Rajya Sabha, as reported by MediaNama, showed ₹379 crore released in 2025-26 against a revised estimate of ₹800 crore.
As of April, nothing had been released from this year’s ₹1,000 crore budget.
Will it understand Kashmiri?
For readers here, there is a more local question.
Indian AI is sold as AI that understands Indian languages.
But most of the attention goes to Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and Marathi.
Kashmiri work has mostly come from small efforts.
NIT Srinagar’s Gaash Lab ran a national challenge in August to build English-to-Kashmiri translation tools, Kashmir Life reported.
AI4Bharat has put a Kashmiri speech-recognition model on the government’s AIKosh platform.
And a young developer from Pulwama, Saqlain Yousuf, built a Kashmiri chatbot on his own, without funding, as this newspaper reported in February 2025.
If government offices are later told to use only Indian models, people in Kashmir will deal with those systems for forms, complaints and services.
A model that handles Hindi well but stumbles on Kashmiri is not much help in Pulwama or Baramulla.
Bottom Line Wanting our own AI is sensible.
But a rule that forces critical offices to switch before the tools are proven could swap one risk for another.

Before any such order, the government should publish how these models perform on real tests, name which languages they truly support, and admit openly that the chips underneath still come from abroad.
Sovereignty that only covers the software is half a job.
The other half is the hardware underneath, and the languages people here actually speak.

However, the oldest member of the Tata family on the board of the trusts stopped short of indicating whether he would take a more active role, saying any future action would "depend on the situation".
The note argues that the induction of members of the Noel Tata family into the trusts was securing "a degree of control over Tata Sons that was never the settlers' intention.

It is entirely inappropriate for more than one family member to serve on a given trust; doing so effectively confers ownership rights over the trusts' significant shareholding in Tata Sons at no consideration whatsoever."

The note also criticises amendments to Tata Sons' articles of association in 2013-14, saying they "fundamentally overturned" the earlier separation between the charitable trusts and Tata Sons' commercial operations by granting the Trusts' chairman veto powers and the ability to appoint directors.

The note further criticises the introduction of a "four-year time limit on the tenure of certain trustees while exempting others", arguing that it "compromised trustee independence and concentrated authority, enabling the marginalisation or removal of trustees who dissent." As an example, it cites the "targeting" of Venu Srinivasan "because he opposed the induction of Noel's son into the Sir Ratan Tata Trust, alongside the earlier removal of Vijay Singh for authoring a factual article." It also backs the continuation of Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran, noting that he had received "overwhelming support" and delivered record earnings and dividend payouts.

The note also argued that listing Tata Sons was "all the more critical" because it would "dismantle the pervasive culture of secrecy", impose greater accountability and increase scrutiny of the group's governance structure.
Jimmy's status as a perpetual trustee also places him at the centre of the governance discussion.
Apart from Jimmy, SRTT's perpetual trustees are Jehangir H C Jehangir and Noel.

stories.headline: Sand extraction surges 142% in J&K in one year
stories.title: Sand extraction surges 142% in J&K in one year
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 16: Sand and gravel extraction in Jammu and Kashmir increased by nearly 142 per cent, from 4.7 lakh tonnes in 2021 to 11.4 lakh tonnes in 2023, according to a research paper published in the Central University of Kashmir Law Review, which has raised concerns over the expansion of mechanised riverbed mining and its impact on Kashmir's rivers. The study, citing figures attributed to the Jammu and Kashmir Department of Geology and Mining, states that extraction rose from approximately 0.47 million tonnes to 1.14 million tonnes during the period, with 72 mining blocks reported as having been put up for auction. The increase of 6.7 lakh tonnes represents a 142.6 per cent rise over the earlier figure, pointing to a substantial expansion in the volume of riverbed material extracted. The findings form part of a research paper titled Illegal Sand Mining in River Jhelum in Jammu and Kashmir: Environmental Law and Governance Challenges, published in Central University of Kashmir Law Review. Authored by Syedah Fatima Zahara Jafri, Syed Irfan Haider Jafri and Mirza Juned Beg, the paper examines changes in mineral extraction, environmental damage and weaknesses in the regulation of mining activities along the Jhelum and its tributaries. The researchers observe that sand and gravel extraction in Kashmir has undergone a major change, moving from small-scale manual collection by local communities to commercial operations involving heavy machinery. The paper traces this transition to growing demand for construction materials, expansion of infrastructure projects and changes in the allocation of mining leases. It states that the widening of the Srinagar–Jammu National Highway and the construction of bridges, tunnels and other infrastructure increased demand for sand, gravel and crushed stone, encouraging the expansion of mechanised extraction. According to the study, traditional extraction practices were generally seasonal and limited in scale, while commercial operations introduced excavators, dredgers and large vehicles capable of removing substantially greater quantities of material. The researchers also refer to an earlier expansion in the number of mineral blocks offered for auction. Citing an auction status report attributed to the Department of Geology and Mining, the paper states that more than 100 minor-mineral blocks had been offered for open bidding by 2019–20. It identifies Pulwama, Budgam and Kulgam among the districts where mechanised extraction has been associated with riverbank erosion and instability. According to the researchers, the removal of sand and gravel at excessive depths can alter river channels, disturb sediment movement and weaken the natural support of riverbanks. The paper also raises concerns about the effects of deep excavation on groundwater recharge, irrigation systems and aquatic habitats. It cites a 2023 report attributed to the University of Kashmir's Environmental Policy Group, which associated mechanised excavation with a 15–18 per cent decline in groundwater levels in affected areas of Pulwama and Budgam. The researchers further identify the loss of fish breeding grounds and damage to wetlands as consequences of changes in riverbeds and sediment distribution. The study refers to environmental concerns in the Rambiara and Veshaw rivers, where deep excavation has been linked to damage to aquatic habitats. It also points to reports of declining water quality and the drying of traditional springs in mining-affected areas. While the increase in extraction reflects the growing demand for construction materials, the researchers question whether environmental monitoring and enforcement have kept pace with the expansion of mining activity. The paper observes that mining leases are subject to environmental clearances and restrictions intended to protect riverbanks, embankments and nearby infrastructure. However, it cites reports of extraction at night, use of heavy machinery near sensitive river stretches and operations outside approved mining areas. The researchers identify inadequate monitoring and poor coordination among departments as major weaknesses in the implementation of mining regulations. They argue that environmental safeguards must be assessed not only at the time mining leases are issued but throughout the period of extraction. The study recommends the use of GPS-based monitoring, digital records of mineral transportation and regular inspections to detect excavation beyond approved limits. It also calls for environmental assessments that examine the cumulative impact of mining on groundwater, fisheries, agriculture and flood vulnerability. The researchers maintain that greater public access to mining and environmental compliance records would help improve accountability. They also recommend involving local communities in monitoring riverbed extraction and reporting suspected violations.
